newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Four frontrunners battle to lead Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Four frontrunners battle to lead Hong Kong.

text.p: Four front-runners are jostling for the role as Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader after nominations closed on Monday without a last-minute strong contender emerging.

More than 30 candidates -- all but four of them complete unknowns and not taken seriously -- put their names forward for the post of chief executive to take over from outgoing British colonial governor Chris Patten.
More than a century and a half of British rule ends at midnight on June 30, when the territory of 6.3 million people will be handed over to China.
China has promised that Hong Kong people, and not cadres from the mainland, will run the territory, but they will not be able to pick the next leader in a general election.

The names of the would-be leaders now go to a China-picked Preparatory Committee, which is in the process of selecting a 400-strong Selection Committee charged with choosing the future leader by December.
Beijing pledged in a 1984 Sino-British treaty that the people of Hong Kong will be permitted to maintain their existing freedoms and way of life for 50 years.
The future Hong Kong administration will be led by a chief executive who will enjoy powers and privileges similar to those accorded to the 28 governors appointed by the British.
Officials handed out 32 application forms for the chief executive post and 31 were returned, Fei Fih, deputy-director of the Preparatory Committee secretariat office, told reporters.
Only four applicants are taken seriously in Hong Kong.

Billionaire shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa, outgoing Chief Justice Sir Ti Liang Yang, businessman Peter Woo and former Appeal Court Judge Simon Li have all launched lavish campaigns in an effort to show they can garner popular support even though the winner will be selected and not elected.
Hong Kong has largely ignored the unknowns -- even one who made the bizarre claim to be the adopted son of China's top official on Hong Kong matters.
Whoever is named by the Selection Committee in December faces a tought balancing act.

The outgoing colonial administration has promised the chief executive designate its full cooperation -- but the British government refuses to have anything to do with a provisional Hong Kong legislature which China plans to set up.
China, angered by electoral reforms spearheaded by Patten, has vowed to dismantle the Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council and replace it with a provisional chamber.

Pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong have accused Beijing of seeking to snuff out Hong Kong's nascent democracy movement. Britain calls the move unnecessary and has lobbied China to let the elected legislature, returned last year, serve out its four year term.
The Selection Committee, in addition to choosing the chief executive, is also charged with choosing the future Provisional Legislature and is expected to do so well before the handover.
All four leading candidates have dodged questions on democracy and civil liberties in the territory after the handover but have said they would work with the Provisional Legislature.
